notes: M2.5 Nigeria human semantic review. Hardening I (NG-B1/B6/B7) rows HCR-NG-001..008 remain frozen. Hardening II (NG-B2/NG-B3) rows HCR-NG-009..024 close CC-NG-ACC-001..016. Classification only: not adopted, not project-claim statuses, not a publication flip. Legacy comparative account propositions remain rejected as formulations. FX Manual 2026 operational domiciliary rules remain unresolved.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Transportation of cash or negotiable instruments in excess of US$10,000 or its equivalent by individuals into Nigeria shall be declared to the Nigeria Customs Service.
reviews.rationale: Entry limb of MLPPA 2022 s.3(3) is supported. Declared bounded_normalization splits the statutory 'in or out of Nigeria' phrase into an atomic entry candidate and preserves the statutory operator 'in excess of' (>). This establishes a declaration obligation only; it does not establish a physical carriage ceiling.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Transportation of cash or negotiable instruments in excess of US$10,000 or its equivalent by individuals out of Nigeria shall be declared to the Nigeria Customs Service.
reviews.rationale: Exit limb of MLPPA 2022 s.3(3) is supported independently of the entry candidate. Statutory operator remains 'in excess of' (>). Exit declaration is established; a general outbound carriage ceiling is not.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: False declaration or failure to make the required declaration to the Nigeria Customs Service is an offence that may lead on conviction to forfeiture of the undeclared funds or negotiable instrument, imprisonment for at least two years, or both.
reviews.reviewed_text: Any person who falsely declares or fails to make a declaration to the Nigeria Customs Service under section 12 of the Foreign Exchange (Monitoring and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act commits an offence and is liable on conviction to forfeit the undeclared funds or negotiable instrument or to imprisonment for a term of at least two years or both.
reviews.rationale: As written, 'may lead' softens MLPPA 2022 s.3(5) liability wording. Bounded reviewed_text restores the statutory 'commits an offence and is liable on conviction' formulation and retains the FEMMPA s.12 cross-reference from the same excerpt. The omitted s.3(4) Customs-to-CBN/Unit reporting chain remains a separate proposition and is not adopted here.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The reviewed official CBN guidance states that the declaration rule for cash or negotiable instruments above US$10,000 does not itself prohibit genuinely owned or obtained funds above that amount from being brought into Nigeria or taken outside the country.
reviews.rationale: Supported as a bounded negative reading of the CBN circular: the declaration rule itself is not a prohibition on genuinely owned funds above the threshold. The candidate already uses 'does not itself prohibit' and therefore does not claim unrestricted carriage, absence of other restrictions, or a without-limit absolute.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Where foreign currency in excess of US$10,000 is imported in cash and deposited into a domiciliary account with an authorised dealer, the account may only be withdrawn from in cash and that imported cash is exportable from Nigeria only in cash.
reviews.reviewed_text: Where a person imports foreign currency in excess of US$10,000 or its equivalent in cash and not by means of a bank draft, mail or telegraphic transfer and deposits the foreign currency in a domiciliary account with an authorised dealer, withdrawals from that account may be made only in cash, and that imported cash is exportable from Nigeria only in cash.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA 1995 s.21(1)-(2) is narrow. The original candidate omitted the cash-not-transfer condition in s.21(1). Bounded reviewed_text restores that condition from the same excerpt and keeps the rule limited to imported cash deposited in a domiciliary account. It must not be generalised into a universal outbound traveller rule, amount-declared-on-entry ceiling, or universal authorised-dealer-document requirement.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The importation and exportation of the naira remain prohibited except as permitted under guidelines issued from time to time by the Central Bank.
reviews.rationale: Direct restatement of FEMMPA 1995 s.14. Supported as the prohibition baseline only. Hardening I-B established that no current primary CBN guideline setting a live numeric traveller exception was pinned; therefore this candidate must not be read as establishing N10,000, N20,000, N100,000, or any other numeric exception.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Current Customs operational guidance uses a declaration trigger of US$10,000 or more, which conflicts with the statutory phrase in excess of US$10,000.
reviews.reviewed_text: Current Customs operational guidance on the e-currency declaration form uses a declaration trigger of US$10,000 or more / equal to or greater than US$10,000.
reviews.rationale: Special review closed. The direct NCS e-CDF excerpt supports only the operational >= trigger. The candidate's assertion that this 'conflicts with' the statute synthesises beyond that single excerpt. Bounded reviewed_text retains the Customs operational operator (>=) only. Dual-operator preservation against MLPPA 2022 s.3(3) (>) remains an I-B source-layer disposition and must not be flattened into one synthetic universal threshold in this candidate.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The earlier Foreign Exchange Act wording requiring declaration only when foreign currency exceeds US$5,000 is a legacy threshold retained for temporal audit and should not be used as the current border-cash rule while MLPPA 2022 is operative.
reviews.reviewed_text: FEMMPA 1995 section 12 states that foreign currency in excess of US$5,000 or its equivalent, whether being imported into or exported out of Nigeria, shall be declared on the prescribed form for reasons of statistics only. That older threshold wording is retained for temporal audit and must not drive the current border-cash declaration threshold while MLPPA 2022 section 3(3) uses in excess of US$10,000.
reviews.rationale: Special review closed. As written, the candidate compressed the FEMMPA s.12 text and asserted temporal supersession without restoring the statistical-declaration pinpoint. Bounded reviewed_text restores the s.12 statistical declaration wording and preserves the Hardening I temporal disposition that this older US$5,000 threshold must not drive current public declaration wording while MLPPA 2022 s.3(3) remains the operative AML/customs declaration text.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Any person may open, maintain and operate a domiciliary account designated in foreign currency with an Authorised Dealer.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA 1995 s.17(1) directly supports domiciliary-account opening with an Authorised Dealer. Supported as account-opening permission only. Does not establish unrestricted FX access, unrestricted international transfer, unrestricted physical FX holding, absence of KYC, or absence of all regulatory limits.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The foreign currency in which a domiciliary account may be opened, maintained and operated shall be any internationally convertible currency.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA 1995 s.17(2) directly supports internationally convertible currency denomination for domiciliary accounts. Currency rule only; not a transfer or holding entitlement.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Except as provided under any other enactment or law, a person making an application to open a domiciliary account under this Act shall not be obliged to disclose the source of the foreign currency sought to be deposited in the account.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA 1995 s.17(3) is supported with the statutory exception limb preserved: source disclosure is not obliged except as provided under any other enactment or law. Special review closed. Does not establish unrestricted funding or that KYC/AML source-of-funds checks never apply.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: A person may open more than one domiciliary account under this Act designated in the same or different foreign currencies and at the same or in different banks.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA 1995 s.17(4) directly supports multiple domiciliary accounts in the same or different currencies and banks. Multiple-account permission only.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: An exporter of goods, including petroleum products, shall open and maintain a foreign currency domiciliary account into which may be retained foreign currency corresponding to the entire proceeds of the export concerned.
reviews.rationale: FEMMPA 1995 s.19 directly supports the exporter-specific obligation to open and maintain a foreign-currency domiciliary account for export proceeds. Kept as a separate account class; not generalised to ordinary domiciliary accounts. FX Manual 2026 export-proceeds operational restrictions remain outside this candidate.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: For external and non-resident non-Nigerian customers, financial institutions shall satisfy themselves that the customer is permanently resident outside Nigeria, and the eligible classes for external accounts are embassies, high commissions, legations or consulates, their career and established members, and other international organisations recognised and accorded diplomatic status and their expatriate officials.
reviews.rationale: CBN CDD Regulations 2023 reg. 25(1)-(2) supported for external-account eligibility classes (diplomatic / international-organisation). Special review closed. Category-specific only; not a universal non-resident FCY entitlement.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: The eligible classes to open non-resident accounts under the CBN Customer Due Diligence Regulations are overseas correspondence and examination bodies, foreign companies executing approved contracts in Nigeria, and foreign professional bodies.
reviews.rationale: CBN CDD Regulations 2023 reg. 25(4) supported for the three listed non-resident account eligible classes. Special review closed. Does not support 'all non-residents may open FCY accounts' or comparative freer-transfer wording.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: All accounts of Non-resident stipulated for the external-account and non-resident-account eligible classes shall, on completion of the contract or the applicant’s business in Nigeria, be closed and the balance on the account, if any, transferred to the customer’s account in country of residence, after proper documentation.
reviews.reviewed_text: All accounts of Non-resident stipulated in subregulations (2) and (4) of regulation 25 of the CBN Customer Due Diligence Regulations, 2023, shall, on completion of the contract or the applicant's business in Nigeria, be closed and the balance on the account, if any, transferred to the customer's account in country of residence, after proper documentation.
reviews.rationale: CDD reg. 25(7) closure rule is supported but the candidate compressed the subregulation cross-reference. Bounded reviewed_text restores the subregulation (2) and (4) pinpoint so closure remains limited to those eligible classes. Special review closed. Not a universal non-resident closure rule.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Where a customer wishes to open a domiciliary account or make a wholesale deposit by cash or inter-bank transfer, a financial institution shall obtain identification evidence appropriate to individuals, companies, or professional intermediaries, and where funding is by inter-bank transfer the institution shall satisfy itself that the transferring institution is regulated for ML, TF or PF prevention in its country of origin.
reviews.rationale: CBN CDD Regulations 2023 reg. 40 supported as bank identification / KYC for domiciliary opening or wholesale cash/inter-bank deposit. Special review closed. Explicit boundary: bank KYC / customer identification is not CBN prior regulatory approval to open a domiciliary account and does not recreate legacy 'CBN approval required' wording.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Effective 1 January 2025, eligible Non-Resident Nigerians may own a Non-Resident Nigerian Ordinary Account or a Non-Resident Nigerian Investment Account subject to meeting KYC requirements, without prejudice to Memorandum 17 of the CBN Foreign Exchange Manual (2018).
reviews.rationale: CBN 2025 NRNOA/NRNIA circular introduction supported for eligible Non-Resident Nigerians from 1 January 2025 subject to KYC, with the Memorandum 17 (2018) without-prejudice exception preserved. Special review closed. Not generalised to all non-residents, foreign nationals, foreign companies, or temporary visitors.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: A Non-Resident Nigerian Ordinary Account enables Non-Resident Nigerians to remit their foreign earnings to Nigeria and manage funds in both foreign and local currencies; account holders may maintain both a foreign-currency account and/or a Naira account.
reviews.rationale: NRNOA purpose and dual-currency structure supported from the CBN framework excerpt. Special review closed. NRNOA-only; conversion and repatriation limbs remain in separate candidates.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: A Non-Resident Nigerian Investment Account enables Non-Resident Nigerians to invest in assets in Nigeria in either foreign currency or local currency, and account holders may maintain both a foreign-currency account and/or a Naira account for that purpose.
reviews.rationale: NRNIA investment-purpose account class supported from the CBN framework excerpt. Special review closed. Distinct from NRNOA; not generalised beyond Non-Resident Nigerians.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: On 15 May 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria officially launched the Fourth Edition of its Foreign Exchange Manual.
reviews.rationale: CBN Reforms page launch statement for Foreign Exchange Manual Fourth Edition (15 May 2026) is supported as temporal meta only. Special review closed. Does not supply or resolve ordinary-vs-export domiciliary operational rules, Form A mechanics, or export cash-withdrawal restrictions; those remain unresolved pending a pinned Manual PDF.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: In cases that are not classified under the external-account or non-resident-account eligible classes in the CBN Customer Due Diligence Regulations, financial institutions shall refer to the Central Bank of Nigeria for clarification.
reviews.rationale: CDD reg. 25(8) clarification-referral rule supported for cases not classified under the external-account or non-resident-account eligible classes. Special review closed. Narrow referral only — not converted into 'all non-resident accounts require CBN approval'.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Balances in the foreign-currency account of a Non-Resident Nigerian Ordinary Account can be fully repatriated out of Nigeria without restriction.
reviews.rationale: CBN NRNOA framework 1.4 directly states FCY balances can be fully repatriated out of Nigeria without restriction. Supported with subject limited to NRNOA foreign-currency account balances. Special review closed. Not expanded to all non-resident accounts, all FCY accounts, all capital or investment funds, or resident accounts.

reviews.candidate_text_snapshot: Non-Resident Nigerian Ordinary Account holders may maintain a Naira account with funds remitted directly from offshore or convertible from a foreign-currency account at prevailing exchange rates through authorised dealers.
reviews.rationale: CBN NRNOA framework currency/conversion limb supported: Naira account funded from offshore remittance or conversion from FCY via authorised dealers. Funding-channel rule for NRNOA only; not a general unrestricted-funding proposition and not an FX Manual 2026 local-deposit schedule.
